Hi Mark. Last class you learned how to admit the other side inside one sentence. Today you learn how to say how big a difference is, and then you put the whole of Phase 3 into three minutes of your own speech. Here is the problem the lesson solves. The word better is true and empty. If I tell you that Northwind is better than Deep Harbor, you still have no idea whether that race was close or whether it was over in March, and the listener has to guess. English fixes this with a small word in front of the comparison, and that word is never the adjective. For a big gap you have far, much, considerably and a lot. Far more ambitious. Much better. Considerably shorter. For a small gap you have marginally, slightly and a little. Marginally shorter than the other two. Slightly less polished. And for first place with nothing near it, you have by far and easily in front of a superlative. By far the best game of the year. Easily the most original thing I played. Then there is the other family, the one that uses as. Nowhere near as generous as Northwind, for a big gap measured downwards. Not quite as sharp as the first one, for the gap that is almost nothing. And every bit as clever as the expensive ones, which means no gap at all, said with force. One more, and it is the one that sounds most like a native speaker. The longer you play it, the thinner the story gets. Each half opens with the, and the comparative comes first in both halves. Now the three traps. First, never mark a comparative twice. More better and most easiest do not exist in English, and the size word goes in front instead. Second, once a sentence opens with as, it has to close with as, never with than. Nowhere near as polished as Northwind. Never as polished than Northwind. Third, and this one comes straight from Portuguese, very never stands in front of a comparative. In Portuguese you say muito melhor and the same word does both jobs. In English you take much, far or a lot. Much better, never very better. Before class, write three sentences about three things you played or watched this year, and use a different size structure in every one. See you in class, Mark.

Right, so before I give you my three, let me tell you what I was measuring, because otherwise the order means nothing. My question was simple. Did I go back to it a second time without anybody asking me to. Not whether I enjoyed it in the first week. Whether I came back. So. First place is the series, and I know that surprises people who expected me to say the game. I have watched it three times now and it still holds up, and the third time I noticed things the first two had hidden from me. The game, which everybody assumed would win, was thrilling exactly once. I opened it again in August and it was lackluster, and I could not tell you why, except that once you know where everything is there is nothing underneath. So the game goes second. It is nowhere near as rewarding the second time as the series is, although I admit it is by far the better thing to play for a weekend. Third place is the one nobody I know has heard of. It is a small book that flew under the radar completely, it was on no list anywhere, and it is nowhere near as ambitious as the other two. It is also far more original than either of them, and I have been back to it twice. Now the honest part. If my question had been which one gave me the best single evening, the order would be exactly backwards, and the game would be first by a distance. That is why I said my benchmark out loud before I said a single title. Change the question and you change the list, and anybody who gives you a ranking without telling you what they measured is asking you to trust them instead of arguing with them.

First, name the benchmark before you name a single title, because an order without a question behind it is just a list of things you like and nobody can argue with it. Then give first place and one reason in a single sentence, so that the strongest thing you have to say arrives while the listener is still paying attention. After that, defend second and third place, and in each one say how big the gap is, since a ranking only becomes interesting when somebody tells you whether the race was close. Next, concede the one thing your winner does worse than the others, because a person who has nothing bad to say about their own choice sounds like an advertisement. Finally, say which one will still hold up in five years and then stop talking, because the last sentence is the one the listener remembers.
